papers.title: Aperiodic dynamics track cortical state shifts during sleep K-complexes.
papers.abstract: Sleep microarchitecture is defined by brief electrophysiological events such as K-complexes (KCs), which are traditionally interpreted as discrete oscillatory phenomena involved in sleep maintenance, sensory gating, and cortical down-states. However, electroencephalography (EEG) also contains aperiodic, broadband activity that reflects non-oscillatory population dynamics and varies systematically across sleep stages. Because KCs are large, low-frequency transient waveforms, they also manifest across a broader frequency range, which creates a bidirectional measurement problem in which discrete events and aperiodic activity are difficult to disentangle. This is because aperiodic dynamics alone can generate fluctuations that resemble KCs, while conversely, the KC waveform itself can inflate the low-frequency end of the spectrum, steepening the fitted exponent even when the underlying aperiodic state is unchanged. These confounds blur what constitutes a real KC and a real aperiodic change in the presence of a KC. A KC-locked change in the aperiodic exponent could therefore reflect a genuine cortical state shift, a measurement artifact from the waveform biasing the spectral fit, or both. Here, we use time-resolved spectral parameterization of overnight sleep EEG to characterize aperiodic dynamics around expert-annotated KCs, with a series of controls designed to separate genuine aperiodic state changes from waveform artifacts. A component of the KC-locked aperiodic change survives these controls, suggesting that KCs are accompanied by a genuine shift toward a higher-exponent, inhibition-dominated cortical state. These findings establish aperiodic activity as a meaningful index of state dynamics during KCs and highlight measurement confounds that any event-locked spectral analysis of large transients must consider. The aperiodic component of neural activity is an increasingly used marker of brain state, yet accurately measuring it around transient events is difficult. Sharp waveforms create broadband power and can masquerade as changes in the underlying dynamics. We address this problem using the sleep K-complex, the largest event in healthy human EEG. Combining four complementary strategies, we disentangle waveform-induced spectral distortion from genuine modulation of aperiodic activity, and show for the first time that K-complexes are accompanied by a transient shift in the aperiodic exponent. Beyond this finding, our framework provides a general method to control for biases that waveform shape introduces into spectral estimates, informing an active debate over how transient events are detected in neural signals.

papers.title: The development of slow and fast theta oscillations in the human brain.
papers.abstract: Theta oscillations are pivotal for attention and memory, with developmental shifts in theta activity and connectivity tracking memory ability across the lifespan. Building on initial evidence that the theta band separates into slow and fast sub-bands across development within the medial temporal lobe (MTL) and the prefrontal cortex (PFC), this preregistered study ( https://osf.io/gsru7 ) characterized the frequencies of slow (∼1.5-4.5 Hz) and fast (∼4.5-9.0 Hz) theta oscillations across the brain in a large developmental cohort. We analyzed intracranial EEG (iEEG) recordings from widespread brain regions in 101 children and adults (5.93-54.00 years, 63 males; n electrodes = 5691) using task-based (attention to to-be-remembered visual stimuli) and task-free (resting-state) data. We reveal distinct slow and fast theta oscillations in all regions and identify a spatial gradient in both frequency ranges, with slow theta oscillations speeding up and fast theta oscillations slowing down from posterior to anterior regions. The dissociation between slow and fast theta frequencies peaks during young adulthood, mirroring the developmental trajectory of attention and memory. In the hippocampus and PFC, attentional state (task-based, task-free) modulated age effects, and individual differences in task-based slow theta frequencies predicted individual differences in memory performance, linking the development of slow theta oscillations to the development of memory. Gray matter volume was not associated with age- or task-related differences in theta frequencies, suggesting that the development of theta oscillations is independent of regional brain structure. This study establishes developmental trajectories of slow and fast theta oscillations in localized brain regions and links the maturation of hippocampal and PFC slow theta oscillations to the development of attention and memory.

papers.title: All Roads Lead to Rome: Resting-State Criticality as a Neurophysiological Marker of Brain-Computer Interface (BCI) Performance in People with Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis (ALS) and Healthy Participants.
papers.abstract: This exploratory study investigates the relationship between resting-state brain dynamics (EEG) and subsequent brain-computer interface (BCI) performance in people with amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) and healthy participants. Grounded in the critical brain hypothesis, we examined whether neurophysiological markers of criticality in resting-state EEG correlate with subsequent BCI performance. We analyzed neuronal avalanche dynamics, multiscale criticality measures, the spectral slope, and Lempel-Ziv complexity across two datasets: a longitudinal single-case study of a person in the locked-in state after a disease history with ALS (Dataset 1) and longitudinal data from 5 people with ALS and single sessions from 6 healthy participants (Dataset 2). Neuronal avalanche dynamics, the spectral slope, and Lempel-Ziv complexity consistently correlated with subsequent BCI performance in people with ALS. Conversely, healthy participants showed inverted correlation patterns for the neuronal avalanche dynamics. While group comparisons were not statistically significant, effect size analyses indicated supercritical brain dynamics in people with ALS. We integrate these findings into the B-ARC (BCI-Aptitude through Resting-State Criticality) framework proposing an inverted U-shaped relationship between the proximity of resting-state brain activity to criticality and BCI control. In this framework, healthy participants approach the critical optimum from a subcritical regime, while people with ALS appear to approach it from a putatively supercritical regime characterized by cortical hyperexcitability. These findings and the proposed framework provide potential resting-state predictors of BCI aptitude in people with ALS and may inform the detection of so-called Windows of Consciousness .

papers.title: LTPat-based SOXFE: A self-organized explainable feature engineering model for automated fibromyalgia detection.
papers.abstract: BackgroundFibromyalgia is a chronic pain disorder associated with sleep disturbance and substantial functional burden.ObjectiveThis study evaluated a self-organized explainable feature engineering (SOXFE) model for EEG-based fibromyalgia classification.MethodsA previously reported sleep EEG dataset from a 32-participant source cohort was analyzed separately for NREM Stage 2 and Stage 3. The analysis-ready version contained 136 labeled stage-record files: 74 for Stage 2 and 62 for Stage 3. The SOXFE model comprised LTPat feature extraction, training-only CWNCA feature selection, tkNN classification, IMV information fusion, and DLob-based explanation. Record-wise LORO was primary; segment-level 10-fold cross-validation was complementary.ResultsRecord-wise LORO used 74 outer folds for Stage 2 and 62 for Stage 3. Descriptive pooled held-out-epoch accuracy was 92.77% (95% CI: 91.76-93.67) for Stage 2 and 97.00% (95% CI: 96.22-97.63) for Stage 3. Every epoch from the held-out recording was excluded from training and selection. Complementary segment-level 10-fold cross-validation yielded 100.00% accuracy for both stages but was not used as evidence of record-wise generalization.ConclusionsThe model provided record-disjoint classification and traceable model-derived explanations in this single-source dataset. LORO prevented within-record epoch leakage. However, participant linkage was unavailable, so records from the same person may have occurred across outer partitions and the reported values may overestimate person-independent performance. Verified subject-wise validation is required before clinical use.

papers.title: Combined population and patient-specific brain networks predict electrical stimulation propagation.
papers.abstract: Cortico-cortical evoked potentials (CCEPs) are used during intracranial EEG (iEEG) monitoring to probe effective connectivity and guide epilepsy surgery. However, the factors governing spatial distribution and variability of stimulation-evoked responses across patients remain incompletely understood, making it difficult to distinguish physiological variation from pathological responses. We aimed to develop interpretable models of CCEP responses that integrate normative and patient-specific features, and to assess how these relationships are influenced by distance, brain-state, and epileptogenicity. We analyzed single-pulse stimulation data from 34 patients with drug-resistant epilepsy undergoing stereo-EEG monitoring. Significant CCEP responses were defined using N1 peak amplitude. For each stimulation-response pair, we derived multimodal features capturing Euclidean distance, effective connectivity priors from F-TRACT, a published population atlas of CCEP response probabilities, normative structural connectivity and communication metrics, and patient-specific functional connectivity estimated from iEEG during baseline and pre-stimulation periods. Lasso-regularized logistic regression models were trained to predict response using leave-one-patient-out cross-validation, and feature importance was examined across spatial scales and seizure onset zone (SOZ) involvement. Performance to predict stimulation-evoked responses improved with the integration of multiple feature domains, with the full model achieving the highest accuracy (median AUC = 0.84). Feature relevance varied with spatial scale: short-range responses were dominated by distance and normative priors, whereas long-range responses depended strongly on patient-specific functional connectivity, especially when measured from pre-stimulation periods. Prediction errors were significantly higher for stimulation-response pairs within the SOZ, indicating deviations from normative connectivity-response relationships in epileptogenic networks. CCEP responses reflect an interaction between spatial constraints, network architecture, and patient-specific brain state. Multimodal modeling of CCEPs provides a principled framework to interpret stimulation responses and may offer complementary markers for identifying epileptogenic networks during presurgical evaluation.

papers.title: The EEG multi-scale brain network and high-order synergy changes in disorders of consciousness during general anesthesia.
papers.abstract: Brain network alterations during general anesthesia (GA) have been extensively investigated in individuals with intact consciousness. However, network dynamics in patients with disorders of consciousness (DoC) under anesthetic perturbation remain poorly understood. We recorded electroencephalogram (EEG) signals from 33 DoC patients (16 UWS and 17 MCS) during GA across three states (DoC-Resting, DoC-MOSSA, and DoC-Recovery). A multi-scale brain network framework was proposed. Low-order network characteristics were assessed using unbiased minimum spanning tree (MST) and directed phase lag index (dPLI), while high-order organization was evaluated using topological data analysis (TDA) and high-order mutual information (HO-MI). UWS patients exhibited a fragmented, line-like topological backbone with lower leaf fraction (p < 0.05) and tree hierarchy (p < 0.05) than MCS patients. dPLI analysis revealed impaired prefrontal top-down directional communication in UWS patients, whereas MCS patients showed transient disruption and recovery of frontoparietal directional organization during anesthesia. Under anesthesia, TDA revealed reduced H1 maximum Betti number in UWS patients (p < 0.01), indicating impaired topological resilience, while MCS patients showed relatively preserved network organization. Furthermore, HO-MI analysis showed increased total correlation with redundant information processing in UWS patients during anesthesia, whereas MCS patients restored synergistic information integration within the central-parietal network during recovery. GA reveals distinct scale-dependent network alterations between MCS and UWS patients. Persistent impairment of directed communication and high-order synergistic integration characterizes disrupted network organization in UWS. The proposed multi-scale EEG framework integrating MST, dPLI, TDA, and HO-MI provides candidate network biomarkers for perioperative consciousness monitoring and assessment in DoC patients. The online version contains supplementary material available at https://doi.org/10.1007/s11571-026-10567-4.

papers.title: A Multi-Domain EEG Framework Integrating Spectral, Functional Connectivity, and Topological Features for Subject-Level ADHD Classification
papers.abstract: Background: Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD) is a common neurodevelopmental disorder characterized by persistent symptoms of inattention, hyperactivity, and impulsivity that significantly affect cognitive, academic, and social functioning. Although electroencephalography (EEG) has emerged as a promising non-invasive tool for identifying objective neurophysiological biomarkers of ADHD because of its high temporal resolution and cost-effectiveness, many existing machine learning studies rely on single-domain EEG features, which may not adequately capture the complex functional organization of the brain. Methods: This study proposes a subject-level EEG classification framework that integrates three complementary feature domains: spectral characteristics, weighted Phase Lag Index (wPLI)-based functional connectivity, and topological descriptors derived from persistent homology. EEG recordings from 121 subjects were preprocessed and segmented into overlapping windows for feature extraction. Window-level features were aggregated to generate subject-level representations. Recursive Feature Elimination (RFE) was employed to select the 110 most informative features from an initial set of 1,043 descriptors. Five machine learning classifiers, including Support Vector Machine (SVM), Random Forest, XGBoost, CatBoost, and Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP), were evaluated using stratified five-fold cross-validation. An ablation study was further conducted to assess the contribution of each feature domain. Model interpretability was investigated using SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) and Local Interpretable Model-agnostic Explanations (LIME), two widely adopted Explainable Artificial Intelligence techniques for interpreting machine learning models. Results: Among the evaluated classifiers, the SVM achieved the highest classification performance, yielding an accuracy of 80.17%, an F1-score of 80.95%, a balanced accuracy of 80.14%, a receiver operating characteristic area under the curve (ROC-AUC) of 86.72%, and a precision recall area under the curve (PR-AUC) of 87.34%. The ablation study demonstrated that combining spectral, functional connectivity, and topological features consistently outperformed individual feature domains, highlighting the complementary nature of these representations. Explainable AI analyses further identified functional connectivity features as the primary contributors to classification performance while confirming the additional value of spectral and topological descriptors. Conclusions: The proposed framework demonstrates that integrating spectral analysis, functional connectivity, and topological data analysis provides an effective and interpretable approach for subject-level ADHD classification from EEG recordings. The combination of recursive feature selection, multi-domain feature fusion, ablation analysis, and Explainable Artificial Intelligence establishes a transparent and reproducible pipeline that may facilitate the development of reliable EEG-based clinical decision-support systems for ADHD.

papers.title: An adaptive, variable-length test for certifying electroencephalographic spike-detection skill: A retrospective feasibility study.
papers.abstract: Determining whether an individual reader has sufficient electroencephalographic (EEG) spike-detection skill is challenging due to limited expert agreement. We evaluated whether modeling skill in interpretable signal-detection terms-discrimination ability separate from response tendency-could power an adaptive, variable-length test that can reliably and efficiently assess reader competence. We analyzed a multirater dataset containing 20 521 EEG segments and 2574 rater sessions. Case signal was estimated from multirater labels, and each reader was modeled using signal-detection parameters: discrimination skill σ and response bias t . Among 368 calibration-eligible raters across five skill tiers, we used a stratified 50/50 train-validation split to select a certification threshold σ ⋆ in training and to apply it in validation. We replayed an adaptive test on each rater's historical responses, using sequential stopping to issue pass, fail, or retest decisions. The training-derived threshold was σ ⋆ = .815 (95% bootstrap confidence interval = .663 - 1.018 , Youden J = .828 ). In validation, pass rates preserved the expected tier ordering: experts 100% ( 14 / 14 ), experienced 100% ( 4 / 4 ), novices 14% ( 1 / 7 ), residents 0% ( 0 / 11 ), and crowd raters 7% ( 11 / 150 ). In the 81-rater adaptive replay, clear failures stopped near 20 trials, and passing experts required a median of 95 trials. Split-half replay showed intraclass correlation coefficient 3 , 1 = .87 for σ ̂ at stopping; there were no hard pass-fail reversals among raters whose two halves both reached decisive verdicts. A signal-detection framework quantified spike-identification skill in EEG readers, and adaptive testing estimated this skill reliably with fewer than 100 short EEG segments. This approach could provide a practical, scalable method for assessing EEG reading competence.

papers.title: What drives intersubject correlation of EEG during auditory narratives?
papers.abstract: When participants are engaged with auditory narratives, physiological and neural signals exhibit temporal correlations between subjects. The intersubject correlation (ISC) increases when attention is directed to the stories, suggesting that shared neural and bodily dynamics arise from a similar processing of the narratives. In this study, we investigated whether the ISC of the EEG elicited by auditory narratives is driven by low-level acoustic (envelope, spectrogram) and/or higher-level linguistic information (word onset, word surprisal) in two groups of healthy participants during passive, attentive and distracted listening. We use temporal response functions (TRFs) for acoustic, and linguistic features to assess the contribution of each feature to the ISC, measured using correlated component analysis (CorrCA). TRFs derived for acoustic features explained a larger fraction of variance in the EEG than linguistic features and were the main contributors to the ISC. The attention-related increase in ISC was driven by all features. Importantly, word surprisal had an effect on ISC only during active story engagement, with timing and scalp distribution consistent with language processing. Notably, the linear responses captured by TRFs only explained a small amount of the overall ISC, suggesting that ISC is largely driven by nonlinear responses to the narratives. Identifying the factors that drive these common neural responses, is clinically relevant for interpreting EEG ISC exhibited in unresponsive patients. We propose that the combined use of ISC and TRFs has the potential to provide meaningful markers of language processing in patients with disorders of consciousness, and we suggest practical recommendations for implementing these approaches in clinical settings.

papers.title: Synchronized audiovisual stimulation enhances neural entrainment: convergent evidence from complementary EEG biomarkers.
papers.abstract: Rhythmic sensory stimulation modulates oscillations via frequency-specific entrainment, but synchronized auditory contributions remain unclear, and periodic-aperiodic decomposition has not been applied to audiovisual entrainment. Forty adults received visual stimulation at 8, 20, and 40 Hz, alone (VF) or synchronized with binaural beats of identical frequencies (VF + BB). EEG was analyzed using power spectral density (PSD), topographical mapping, Sample Entropy (SampEn), Lempel-Ziv Complexity (LZC), Phase-Locking Regularity (PLR), and IRASA to separate periodic (SSVEP) from aperiodic (1/f) contributions. Visual flicker induced frequency-specific entrainment, and binaural beats modulated responses frequency-dependently. At 8 Hz, flicker elicited a periodic SSVEP; adding binaural beats enhanced this component and increased aperiodic activity. At 20 Hz, synchronized audiovisual stimulation enhanced both periodic and aperiodic components. At 40 Hz, IRASA showed no significant periodic modulation; VF + BB produced a widespread increase in aperiodic offset and exponent, absent under VF alone. VF + BB reduced SampEn across all frequencies and increased PLR at 8 and 20 Hz, whereas LZC decreased at 8 Hz and increased at 20 Hz. Synchronized audiovisual stimulation produced frequency-dependent changes in EEG spectral organization. At 8 and 20 Hz, adding binaural beats enhanced the periodic SSVEP component, with changes in the aperiodic background. At 40 Hz, conventional PSD showed increased gamma activity, but periodic-aperiodic decomposition did not reveal significant periodic enhancement; audiovisual stimulation primarily altered aperiodic offset and exponent. Complementary regularity and phase-based measures showed frequency-dependent temporal changes. Findings highlight combining conventional spectral analysis, periodic-aperiodic decomposition, and complementary EEG biomarkers to characterize synchronized audiovisual stimulation.

papers.title: Social attention and coordinated movement produce dissociable spectral and network changes during dyadic improvisational dance.
papers.abstract: Dance is increasingly delivered as an intervention for social and affective functioning, but a live dyadic encounter confounds several distinct ingredients - social attention, verbal engagement, coordinated movement, and in-the-moment generation - so its neural effects cannot be assigned to any one of them. We recorded dual-brain mobile EEG from adult human participants of both sexes (16 female, 2 male) and a dance instructor across six five-minute conditions that vary these ingredients independently: solitary rest, direct eye gaze, conversation, teacher-led and participant-led mirroring, and free improvisation, with concurrent head-mounted accelerometry. Referencing each condition to eye gaze - socially engaging but nearly motionless - rather than to solitary rest partitioned the response. The components proved dissociable. Nonverbal social attention alone reorganized the power spectrum, flattening the aperiodic exponent (g = -0.97) and desynchronizing alpha-band oscillations (g = -0.90), while leaving inter-regional connectivity unchanged (amplitude g = +0.15; phase g = +0.11). Verbal engagement added high-frequency amplitude coupling (g = +2.61) without further spectral change. Coordinated movement added a decrease in theta/alpha coupling involving the frontoparietal-control network (g = -0.59), the signature of an externally directed state, alongside a further spectral shift (g = -0.61). Movement-vigor covariates, corticokinematic coherence, and aperiodic-adjusted power indicated that the spectral effects were cortical rather than myogenic. Four weeks of improvisational dance training increased empathic responsiveness to others' distress relative to a movie control (g = 0.82). Coordinated social movement thus acts on the brain componentially, with mutual attention rather than motor load establishing the engaged state.

papers.title: Enhanced cortical tracking of unfamiliar languages in both monolinguals and bilinguals.
papers.abstract: Humans routinely encounter speech in languages they have never heard, yet how the brain responds to such input and whether bilingual experience shapes this response remains unknown. Here, we used electroencephalography (EEG) and temporal response function (TRF) modeling to examine cortical tracking of the speech envelope in 24 English-monolingual and 24 English-Mandarin bilingual adults. Participants listened to naturally produced continuous speech in three languages: English (familiar to all), Mandarin (familiar to bilinguals only), and Vietnamese (unfamiliar to all). We report two main findings. First, both monolinguals and bilinguals showed enhanced cortical tracking for unfamiliar relative to familiar languages, evidenced by higher EEG prediction accuracy (PA). Monolinguals showed enhanced tracking for both Mandarin and Vietnamese, whereas bilinguals showed enhancement only for Vietnamese, consistent with Mandarin being a familiar language for this group. This finding suggests that enhanced cortical encoding of unfamiliar speech is a general property of the listening brain, not a signature of listening to a non-native language or reduced language proficiency. Second, bilinguals strikingly showed stronger cortical tracking than monolinguals overall, in both PA and TRF peak weights, with the TRF peak weight advantage present across all three languages, suggesting a difference in how bilingual experience shapes the neural encoding of speech. These findings have implications for understanding how the brain navigates the linguistic diversity of everyday life in an increasingly global, multilingual world. More than half the world speaks more than one language, and most people regularly hear speech they cannot understand. How the brain responds to such speech, and whether bilingualism matters, is unclear. We recorded brain activity from monolingual and bilingual adults listening to familiar and unfamiliar speech. Both groups showed enhanced tracking of unfamiliar speech compared to familiar speech and bilinguals showed stronger tracking than monolinguals overall, suggesting a potential difference in how bilingual brains process speech. These findings advance our understanding of how the brain navigates speech in a multilingual world.

papers.title: Transcranial magneto-acoustic stimulation modulates M1-PPN spike-LFP coupling and improves motor dysfunction in parkinsonian rats.
papers.abstract: This study aimed to investigate whether transcranial magneto-acoustic stimulation (TMAS) improves motor dysfunction in Parkinson's disease (PD) model rats and whether its effects are associated with modulation of bidirectional spike-local field potential (LFP) coupling between the primary motor cortex (M1) and the pedunculopontine nucleus (PPN). Two primary cohorts (n = 24 each) comprised WT + Sham, PD + Sham, and PD + TMAS groups (n = 8/group). An independent supplementary healthy-control experiment included newly allocated WT + Sham and WT + TMAS groups (n = 8/group; 16 rats total), both of which followed the Experiment 1 workflow. Pre-treatment APO rotation counts were compared between the two PD groups as a functional index of lesion severity. Motor performance, TH and c-Fos immunofluorescence, and in vivo M1-PPN electrophysiology were evaluated. Spike-LFP coherence and phase-locking value (PLV) were compared among the three primary groups separately within each putative neuronal class, behavioral state, and frequency band. APO rotation counts did not differ between PD + Sham and PD + TMAS rats before treatment in either experiment. TMAS-treated PD rats showed improved behavioral performance, and the pattern of differences in M1-PPN spike-LFP coherence and PLV relative to PD + Sham rats varied across frequency bands, behavioral states, and putative neuronal classes. At the terminal histological assessment, PD + TMAS rats showed a higher proportion of TH-positive cells in the SNc than PD + Sham rats. In the independent healthy-control experiment, WT + TMAS did not significantly differ from WT + Sham in most behavioral indices or TH-positive cell proportion, but it showed a shorter pole-test turning time and a higher c-Fos-positive cell proportion. TMAS ameliorated motor deficits in PD model rats and was associated with frequency band, behavioral-state, and putative-class-dependent changes in M1-PPN spike-LFP coupling. These findings provide preliminary evidence supporting TMAS as a potential noninvasive neuromodulation strategy for PD-related motor dysfunction, while the disease specificity of the electrophysiological effects remains to be established.

papers.title: Intracranial characterization of gamma in humans in response to auditory gratings
papers.abstract: Activity in the gamma frequency range (>30Hz) serves as a neural hallmark of stimulus encoding across multiple sensory modalities. Based on its distinct properties, this activity could be classified as broadband or narrowband oscillations. Visual stimuli, such as a grating, induce narrowband oscillations, which have shown promise as diagnostic markers for neurological disorders. However, such tasks are discomforting for the subjects. These can be made subject-friendly by swapping the stimulus for an auditory one; however, most auditory stimuli elicit a broadband activity. In search of an ideal candidate to induce auditory narrowband oscillations, we previously recorded responses to auditory gratings in electroencephalography (EEG) recordings (Gulati & Ray, 2024) using a passive listening paradigm. We observed a focal sustained broadband increase in high gamma activity (70-150Hz), which was not selective towards any stimulus attributes. Nevertheless, since EEG represents activity of a large population, it remained unclear whether observed activity represented a broadband increase or comprised multiple narrowband rhythms, and whether it was indeed untuned. To elucidate this, we recorded invasively from the regions on and around the superior temporal gyrus, closer to Heschl's gyrus of seven patients undergoing epilepsy resection surgery. Patients were either under anesthesia or fully awake while we presented auditory gratings through loudspeakers. We found a transient increase in broadband gamma activity (30-100Hz) followed by a sustained suppression of beta rhythm (14-28Hz). This broadband gamma was selective for slower spectro-temporal modulations. Our result compares the responses obtained across different recording scales and corroborates that auditory gratings produce broadband but not narrowband gamma activity.

papers.title: Modulation of the speed of Intrinsic Alpha Frequency (IAF) with tACS modulates variability of illusory speech perception
papers.abstract: Navigating the world requires our brains to constantly process a massive influx of information from the environment. One of the most remarkable yet complex feats the human brain performs daily is speech perception. It is a multifaceted, hierarchical process that relies heavily on the integration of auditory and visual cues, particularly in noisy environments. Neural integration of these streams is hypothesized to depend on temporal mechanisms governed by individual alpha frequency (IAF, 8-12 Hz), which serves as a key neural correlate of the temporal binding window (TBW). While IAF has been linked to multisensory integration, its role in shaping multisensory illusions remains largely unexplored. Here, we tested this directly using transcranial alternating current stimulation (tACS) to modulate occipital activity during multisensory conflict. In a two-day protocol involving 27 healthy participants, resting-state EEG was recorded to determine IAF. On Day 2, participants then performed a multisensory speech task involving congruent (pa/, /ta/, /ka/) and incongruent McGurk stimuli (auditory /pa/, visual /ka/), both at baseline and during tACS applied at IAF and offset frequencies (IAF +/- 2 Hz) over occipital electrodes. While accuracy for congruent syllables remained high across conditions, results revealed that tACS significantly reduced the perception of illusory /ta/ percepts during McGurk trials. Finally, using a phenomenological model based on Kuramoto oscillators, we provided a mechanistic explanation for the percentage of illusory responses observed across participants under the influence of tACS at IAF and offsets. This study highlights the potential for targeted neuromodulatory interventions to influence multisensory processing in clinical or professional settings.

papers.title: Brief Trains of Closed-loop TMS Induce Controllable Power in FM-theta Oscillations
papers.abstract: Objective. Frontal-midline theta (FM-theta; 4-8 Hz) oscillations are thought to support cognition. Brief trains of transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS) can probe these oscillations with high temporal precision but have rarely changed theta power. One possible reason is that prior studies ignored the instantaneous phase of the oscillation, which strongly shapes the cortical response to TMS. We tested whether brief TMS trains triggered at specific FM-theta phases in real time directionally modulate post-train FM-theta power. Approach. Six healthy adults received TMS over dorsomedial prefrontal cortex (Fz) with concurrent electroencephalography during a whole-report working memory task. A beamformer and real-time phase-estimation pipeline triggered four-pulse 6 Hz trains (110% of resting motor threshold) at FM-theta peaks (0 degrees) or troughs (180 degrees), randomized trial by trial. Post-train spectral power was decomposed into total, induced (non-phase-locked) and evoked (phase-locked) components. Main results. Trough-triggered trains transiently increased post-train FM-theta power relative to peak-triggered trains; task performance did not differ. Cluster-based permutation tests showed trough-peak differences in total (4.6-7.1 Hz) and induced (5.0-7.8 Hz) power ~50-440 ms after the train, suggesting amplification of the oscillation . No evoked effect was detected. The total-power effect was robust at the subject level (Cohen's dz = 1.32, p = 0.023). Within-train theta power did not differ between conditions, suggesting a cortical origin. Significance. To our knowledge, this is the first study to lock brief rhythmic TMS trains to the real-time phase of an ongoing oscillation, and to show phase-dependent modulation of FM-theta power after individual trains on timescales relevant to behavior. Open-loop brief-train protocols may have missed such effects by mixing faciliatory and suppressive phases. Phase-locked brief trains offer a precise tool for testing the causal role of oscillations in cognition.

papers.title: A touch that lingers: synchronized patting strengthens neural tracking of auditory rhythm in newborns
papers.abstract: Rhythmic auditory stimulation in early life rarely occurs in isolation. Caregivers naturally combine singing and speech with rhythmic touch, rocking, and visual cues. Newborns are sensitive to auditory rhythm from birth, yet little is known about how temporally aligned information across sensory modalities shapes the neural encoding of auditory rhythmic structure. Here, we tested whether rhythmic touch can alter how the newborn brain tracks an ongoing auditory signal beyond the period of tactile stimulation. We recorded high-density electroencephalography from full-term newborns (N = 40), 1-3 days after birth, while they were exposed to recorded French lullabies presented either alone or accompanied by gentle patting synchronized with the metrically strong beat. Patting was delivered intermittently, allowing us to compare neural responses to lullabies across conditions, notably during periods without concurrent tactile stimulation. We quantified neural tracking of the lullabies using brain-stimulus coherence and temporal response function modeling. Newborns' neural activity synchronized with the rhythmic structure of the lullabies at frequencies corresponding to both the beat and the metrically accented strong beat. Critically, neural tracking was stronger when the lullabies had been accompanied by synchronized touch than when they were presented alone, and this enhancement persisted during subsequent periods in which no touch was delivered. Although rhythmic touch enhanced tracking in newborns with both weaker and stronger auditory-only tracking, there was a larger gain in those who initially showed weaker auditory tracking. Together, our findings reveal that the newborn brain exploits rhythmic touch to strengthen its encoding of auditory rhythm, and that this benefit outlasts the touch itself. This provides neural evidence that patting an infant in time with a song, a caregiving practice shared across cultures, does more than simply provide a tactile stimulation. It shapes how the newborn brain encodes the song's rhythm.

papers.title: Pre-treatment EEG microstates and response to antipsychotic drugs in first episode psychosis.
papers.abstract: First-line antipsychotics are ineffective in ∼40% of people with first episode psychosis (FEP). Electroencephalogram (EEG)-based predictive biomarkers could be a scalable solution to reduce trial-and-error. We acquired EEG in 56 minimally treated FEP individuals before treatment initiation, and 34 matched healthy controls (HC). Treatment response was defined as >50% improvement in BPRS scores by 12 weeks of treatment. Modified k-means clustering of resting-state EEG yielded six microstates including canonical topographies (A-D). The first principal component (PC1) of microstate properties derived from HCs served as a normative reference onto which FEP patients were projected. Baseline PC1 was used to predict treatment response in adjusted regression analyses. To test stability of results, a second dataset of HCs (n=92) was fitted using the same microstate solution and compared to our native HC dataset. PC1 scores derived from this independent normative dataset were also used for predicting response in FEP. Individual microstates replicated established patient-control differences (e.g., higher presence of microstate C compared to D, p<0.001). PC1 explained 34.8% of variance. Baseline PC1 predicted subsequent treatment response (adjusted OR=0.63, p<0.001), yielding AUC=72.3% in leave-one-out cross-validation (p perm <0.001) when combined with clinical information. PC1 from our HC transported well to the second healthy control EEG dataset (n=92) (r=0.9,p<0.001; r=0.89,p<0.001 ). PC1 in FEP derived using PC1 weights from a second normative dataset also predicted response in FEP (OR=0.70, p=0.03). EEG microstate architecture differing from the expected norm is associated with lower odds of treatment response in FEP.

papers.title: Prefrontal EEG Delta-Beta Coupling Marks Depressed State in Adult Siblings.
papers.abstract: Major depressive disorder (MDD) is marked by disorganization in electrophysiological brain networks, yet it remains unclear whether such disorganization reflects the state-dependent pathological effects or a trait-like vulnerability. We analyzed resting-state electroencephalographic (EEG) delta-beta phase-amplitude coupling (PAC) in two sibling cohorts. Current-MDD families included individuals with current MDD and their currently unaffected siblings (n=36), and remitted-MDD families comprised individuals with remitted MDD and their lifetime unaffected siblings (n=110). Delta-beta high PAC was significantly elevated (p corr ≤0.05) over the left-medial frontal region in participants with current MDD relative to their unaffected siblings. In the remitted-MDD families, no significant differences were observed. Regrouping all individuals irrespective of family ties into current MDD, remitted MDD, and never-depressed controls confirmed significantly elevated frontal delta-beta high PAC at rest in the current-MDD subgroup compared to other subgroups. Overall, delta-beta high coupling reflects the depressive state rather than a trait-like or familial vulnerability.

papers.title: Hyperexcitable but seizure-free: hippocampal network dysfunction in a Wolfram syndrome model.
papers.abstract: Wolfram syndrome (WS) is a rare, life-limiting progressive neurodegenerative disorder caused by pathogenic variants in the WFS1 gene. It is a prototype endoplasmic reticulum (ER) stress disorder, and the mechanisms underlying neurological phenotypes in WS remain incompletely understood. Although WFS1 protein is abundant in the hippocampus, the role of this region in WS remains relatively understudied. Here we characterize hippocampal function across scales in mice carrying a patient orthologous Wfs1 variant (p.W542*) on both alleles. Male mutants lose excitatory synapses, and dissociated hippocampal neurons are markedly hyperexcitable yet generate no increase in network bursting and no shift in network criticality, indicating that their additional firing is not recruited into coordinated population activity. This finding translates in vivo wherein intracranial electroencephalogram (EEG) recordings show no epileptiform activity or seizures in either sex, with no hippocampal astrogliosis, alongside a male-specific reduction in hippocampal low-gamma power. Additionally, EEG demonstrates a sex-specific disruption of sleep, which parallels a sex-divergent synaptic phenotype. Mutant male mice show impaired hippocampus-dependent fear memory and reduced voluntary motor activity. Taken together, we propose that cellular hyperexcitability in the WS hippocampus does not translate into increased network bursting, potentially due to disproportionate loss of excitatory synapses. This dissociation may provide a functional substrate for the neurological features of WS.

papers.title: Toward A Whole-Brain Interface Enabled by High-Resolution Surface Electrophysiology.
papers.abstract: The goal of building a whole-brain interface-capable of generating a real-time digital representation of the state of the entire central nervous system-has long been framed as a hardware challenge of recording simultaneously from ever-larger numbers of microelectrodes. Advances in high-resolution neural interfaces now enable electrophysiologic interaction with the human nervous system at spatial and temporal resolutions previously unattainable without disrupting tissue architecture or physiology. These capabilities create new opportunities for mechanistic neuroscience, neuroprosthetics, and precision-guided neurosurgery. With the advent of modern microelectrode array technology, however, the whole-brain interface has also become a data challenge. Rather than pursuing large-scale human brain recording purely through a single device placed in a single patient, we demonstrate here that systematic multi-subject aggregation, across brain regions and behavioral paradigms, in a common anatomical framework, can achieve something functionally similar to a whole-brain interface. Here we present an approach to a functional atlas of the human central nervous system derived from high-resolution surface electrophysiology recordings obtained in the first 70 patients implanted with an anatomically conformal, thin-film neural interface positioned in more than 100 locations. The atlas comprises >100,000 electrode deployments and catalogs placement across a broad range of neuroanatomic targets spanning the motor, sensory, language, auditory, and associative domains, as well as brainstem and spinal cord structures that have historically been difficult to access at high electrophysiologic resolution. Across participants, aggregated recordings reveal somatotopic organization, including digit representations that follow a lateral-to-medial ordering consistent with classical homuncular maps, with transitions between adjacent representations occurring over spatial scales of approximately 0.8-2.0 mm; canonical frequency-band signatures, such as movement-related beta-band suppression and focal high-gamma (70-200 Hz) increases during motor and speech behaviors; and task-modulated population dynamics in both evoked and spontaneous activity across cortical, brainstem, and spinal cord regions. These findings yield insight into patterns of mesoscale electrophysiological dynamics conserved across the entire human central nervous system, suggesting that fine-scale functional organization is preserved across individuals when aligned to common anatomical landmarks. We further demonstrate several applications of these high-resolution recordings, including real-time neural decoding from upper extremity motor cortex to enable real-time neuroprosthetic control, and from ventrolateral cortex to decode cortical correlates of spoken language, facial movements, and complex facial expressions of emotion, supporting initial feasibility of combined verbal and nonverbal communication interfaces. Together, these results establish a paradigm for approaching large-scale interfaces with the human brain, as well as a starting point for a scalable, extensible atlas of human electrophysiologic function designed to accelerate discovery across basic neuroscience, translational research, and clinical neurotechnology.

papers.title: A Novel Digital Phenotype of Physical Activity: Associations with Heart Rate Fragmentation
papers.abstract: Background Heart rate fragmentation (HRF) has emerged as a novel marker of sinoatrial instability and neuroautonomic dysregulation and is a predictor of incident cardiovascular disease (CVD) events and cardiovascular mortality. Leveraging heart rate fragmentation as a novel measure may help us better understand the prognostic significance of physical activity. Physical activity (PA) patterns are multidimensional and difficult to study holistically, however. We sought to examine for novel PA clusters in a cohort of veteran men and evaluate their prognostic significance based on their associations with neuroautonomic dysregulation. Methods In this cross-sectional study, we examined 602 male veterans from the Vietnam Era Twins Study of Electrophysiology in Posttraumatic Stress Disorder (VETS-EP) who were enrolled between 2022 and 2026. Accelerometry data were used to derive physical activity parameters across 6 domains: volume, sedentary behavior, intensity, diurnal pattern, fragmentation, and variability. Heart rate fragmentation was assessed using percentage of inflection points (PIP), inverse average length of segments (IALS), percentage of short segments (PSS), and percentage of alternating segments (PAS). Gaussian mixture models were used to derive digital phenotypes of physical activity, and associations with heart rate fragmentation were assessed using linear mixed models. Results Participants had a mean age of 73.8 {+/-} 2.9 years and 93.2% reported White race. Two overlapping phenotypes of physical activity patterns were identified: a compact-early phenotype, characterized by earlier activity timing and slightly greater overall activity, and a diffuse-late phenotype, characterized by later activity timing and greater heterogeneity in activity volume. In fully adjusted models, the diffuse-late phenotype was associated with higher PIP, the primary outcome ({beta}: 1.199, 95% CI: 0.034 to 2.363, p-value: 0.044), and higher IALS ({beta}: 0.01210, 95% CI: 0.00048 to 0.02373, p-value: 0.041), but not PSS or PAS, compared with the compact-early phenotype. Conclusions In older male veterans, Gaussian mixture model phenotyping identified two overlapping physical activity phenotypes, differing mainly in diurnal timing and in the dispersion of overall activity, that were associated with modest differences in heart rate fragmentation. These phenotypes provide a framework for capturing complex physical activity patterns. Future prospective studies representing diverse populations are needed to validate such phenotypes.

papers.title: SIGMA: SIgnaling via Golgi Morphology Analysis for pathway-state classification.
papers.abstract: Organelle morphology is increasingly recognized as a computationally accessible readout of molecular state, yet whether subcellular architecture can identify which signaling pathway is active, not merely whether a cell is perturbed, remains untested. Here we introduce SIGMA (SIgnaling via Golgi Morphology Analysis), a framework that reframes pathway identification as a morphological classification problem centered on the Golgi apparatus. SIGMA integrates imaging flow cytometry for population-scale Golgi profiling, teacher-student knowledge distillation to transfer fine morphological cues from limited high-resolution images to an efficient lower-resolution classifier, and mechanistic generalization testing with chemically distinct activators. Applied to MRC-5 fibroblasts across six conditions spanning four signaling cascades plus controls, SIGMA achieved 90.02% cell-level accuracy and correctly assigned five of seven structurally unrelated external compounds to their expected pathway class. These results establish Golgi morphology as a multiplexed, machine-readable fingerprint of signaling state.

papers.title: EEG Microstates are Not Associated with Psychotic Symptoms, Neurocognitive Domains or Psychosocial Functioning in Adolescents and Young Adults with Clinical High Risk for Psychosis.
papers.abstract: EEG microstates are brief and discrete topographic patterns of electrical brain activity. Microstates last for 60-120 milliseconds, are thought to represent transient, quasi-stable neural networks, and traditionally four distinct classes (A-D) are distinguished. One of the core concepts of present neuroscience is that neuroimaging is able to capture meaningful networks of brain activity, which can be translated into specific cognitive functions. Following this idea, each microstate might correspond to specific core brain functions. Importantly, these cognitive functions are impaired in mental disorders. Clinical high-risk (CHR) refers to a state associated with an increased risk of developing psychosis. Previous research has demonstrated consistent microstate alterations in CHR individuals (especially in class D), as well as in psychosis. However, the neurobiological and functional meaning of microstate alterations in CHR populations is still elusive. Since the CHR state is associated with reduced neurocognition (e.g., processing speed, verbal memory, executive functions) in combination with specific clinical symptoms and impairments in psychosocial functioning, relationships between resting-state microstates and these domains were examined in a large cross-sectional cohort of CHR individuals (n = 100). Contrary to our expectations, no significant correlations were found for these clinical measures. The finding suggests that while microstate parameters may differ between CHR individuals and controls, these alterations do not seem to directly reflect the neurobiology of clinical symptoms or neurocognitive and psychosocial functions. EEG microstate deviations as candidate trait biomarker therefore require further investigation and validation in longitudinal studies to establish their stability and predictive value.

papers.title: The engagement of layer 6 corticothalamic neurons in somatosensation.
papers.abstract: The corticothalamic neurons from layer 6 (L6CT) of primary sensory cortices provide extensive input to the thalamus in addition to projecting across layers intracortically, positioning them to play a key hypothesized role in shaping thalamocortical signaling. With the expansion of tools for precise functional identification of L6CT neurons during in-vivo electrophysiology, increasing evidence highlights L6CT neurons as dynamic gain modulators of thalamocortical sensory responses. However, much of the work to date has been conducted under anesthesia and not in the context of awake and/or behaving animals. In this study, we show in the awake mouse that L6CT neurons convey information about the ascending sensory input, the timing of which is fast enough to contribute to the sensory response of neurons throughout the thalamocortical circuit. Overall, L6CT neurons robustly encode the presence vs absence of a sensory stimulus but are relatively weak encoders of the fine details. Benchmarked against the activity of other excitatory cortical neurons, we also provide evidence for L6CT neurons as predictors of behavioral outcome during a trained detection task. Taken together, the results in this study potentially tie L6CT neurons to behavior in tactile detection, one of the most fundamental functional roles of the pathway. Layer 6 corticothalamic (L6CT) neurons provide one of the major feedback pathways from the sensory cortex to the thalamus, yet the extent to which their role in sensory processing remains poorly understood. We show that L6CT neurons in mouse somatosensory cortex robustly signal the presence of tactile stimuli but are comparatively weak encoders of stimulus strength. During a sensory detection task, their responses strongly reflect whether the animal detects the stimulus and predict behavioral outcome better than other cortical excitatory neurons. These findings suggest that L6CT neurons are specialized less for representing fine sensory detail and more for signaling the occurrence and behavioral relevance of sensory events, providing insight into when and how corticothalamic feedback participates in perception.

papers.title: PRNP D178N-129MM prion disease: Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease-like cortical ribboning without prominent early insomnia.
papers.abstract: The PRNP p.Asp178Asn (D178N) mutation on a methionine-bearing codon-129 allele is classically associated with fatal familial insomnia (FFI), but some carriers develop a Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease (CJD)-like phenotype. We report a 59-year-old woman with two months of rapidly progressive cognitive-language decline, caregiver-observed nocturnal sitting-up and sleep talking, weight loss, extensive cortical diffusion-weighted imaging (DWI) ribboning, positive cerebrospinal fluid 14-3-3, and positive multisite skin real-time quaking-induced conversion. Electroencephalography showed diffuse slowing without periodic sharp-wave complexes. PRNP sequencing identified D178N with methionine homozygosity at codon 129. A focused literature review identified six previously reported individual D178N-129MM cases with prion-compatible cortical or cortical-striatal DWI abnormalities. Because these reports were selectively ascertained by imaging and used heterogeneous clinical assessments, they were not treated as a clinical series or compared numerically with MRI-negative cohorts. Other D178N-129MM reports show normal DWI in non-insomnia cognitive or motor presentations, objective sleep abnormalities preceding insomnia, and occasional cortical DWI hyperintensity in FFI cohorts. D178N-129MM disease shows substantial phenotypic and imaging heterogeneity. Marked CJD-like cortical ribboning can occur in an initially non-sleep-dominant presentation and should not exclude an FFI-associated genotype. MRI pattern alone should not be used to infer a specific clinical phenotype; PRNP sequencing and objective sleep assessment remain important when clinically appropriate.

papers.title: Complementing Engel Classification: Postoperative Scalp EEG as an Objective Indicator in SEEG-Guided Radiofrequency Thermocoagulation-A Seizure-Onset Pattern-Based Stratified Analysis.
papers.abstract: Stereoelectroencephalography-guided radiofrequency thermocoagulation (SEEG-RFTC) is a minimally invasive therapy for drug-resistant focal epilepsy. However, the relationship between specific seizure-onset patterns (SOPs), particularly low-voltage fast activity (LVFA), and postoperative scalp EEG normalization remains inadequately characterized. This study investigates whether LVFA predicts RFTC efficacy and whether postoperative EEG serves as an objective complement to clinical outcome measures. To evaluate LVFA-dominant SOPs as predictors of seizure freedom and scalp EEG normalization after SEEG-RFTC, and to assess their interaction with MRI findings. In a retrospective cohort of 25 patients, seizure-onset patterns (SOPs) were classified as LVFA-present (n = 13) or LVFA-absent (n = 12). Outcomes included Engel classification and 6-month postoperative scalp EEG. Seizure freedom and EEG normalization rates were compared, with MRI-stratified analysis. The seizure-free rate was 92.3% (12/13) in the LVFA-present group versus 33.3% (4/12) in the LVFA-absent group (p = 0.004). EEG normalization was more frequent in LVFA-present patients (7/8, 87.5%) than in LVFA-absent patients (4/12, 33.3%; p = 0.028); all but one patient with EEG normalization was seizure-free, the sole exception being an LVFA-absent patient who remained Engel III. In MRI-negative patients, LVFA-present had 100% (6/6) seizure freedom versus 20.0% (1/5) without LVFA (p = 0.015). Scalp EEG normalization may serve as a relatively objective marker of complete disintegration of the epileptic network, whereas some patients with persistent EEG abnormalities may still achieve seizure freedom with the aid of antiseizure medications. In this cohort, LVFA-present SOPs are strongly associated with favorable RFTC outcomes and may represent a prerequisite for postoperative scalp EEG normalization. Postoperative EEG is a sensitive objective endpoint that complements Engel classification. Systematic PET evaluation in larger cohorts may further refine candidate selection in MRI-negative patients.

papers.title: Long-Term Outcomes of Nonlesional Extratemporal Epilepsy Surgery Using Subdural Grid Implantation.
papers.abstract: Nonlesional extratemporal lobe epilepsy (ETE) remains one of the most challenging forms of drug-resistant epilepsy to treat surgically because seizure onset zones are often poorly defined on conventional neuroimaging. The long-term effectiveness of subdural grid-guided surgery in this population remains incompletely understood. This study aimed to evaluate long-term surgical outcomes in patients with intractable nonlesional extratemporal epilepsy who underwent subdural grid-guided epilepsy surgery. A retrospective study was conducted from January 1, 2014 to December 31, 2024. Clinical, pathological, and invasive electroencephalography data were reviewed. Seizure outcomes were assessed using Engel's classification at 6 months and 2 years after surgery. Fifty-five patients with nonlesional extratemporal epilepsy were included. Seizure freedom (Engel class I) was achieved in 12 patients (21.8%) at 6 months and increased to 30 patients (54.5%) at 2 years. These improvements were not statistically significant ( p = 0.16 and 0.53, respectively). Favorable trends toward better seizure outcomes were observed in patients aged from adolescence to middle adulthood, those with tumor pathology, and those with parietal lobe seizure foci. Subdural grid-guided surgery for nonlesional extratemporal epilepsy resulted in seizure-free rates of 21.8% at 6 months and 54.5% at 2 years, with improvement over time but without statistically significant predictors of outcome.

papers.title: The cognitive cost of artificial intelligence on ageing workforce: Analyzing age-related effects on mental workload and task performance in computer-based environment.
papers.abstract: BackgroundThe current world demographic reality necessitates a critical re-evaluation of how technological tools, specifically those powered by artificial intelligence (AI), interact with the varying cognitive profiles of a ageing workforce.ObjectivesThe objective of this study is to evaluate the spatial distribution of mental workload and objective task performance across AI-assisted and non-AI-assisted conditions in a computer-based environment.MethodAn experimental study involving 30 older workers compared standardized office tasks under non-AI-assisted (Segment A) and AI-assisted (Segment B) conditions. Mental workload was assessed using NASA-TLX, Heart Rate Variability (HRV), and EEG-based Beta-Alpha Ratios (BAR) across frontal (F3, F4), parietal (P3, P4), and occipital (O1, O2) regions. Performance in document preparation (Task 1) and arithmetic operations (Task 2) was evaluated using percentage-based accuracy, efficiency, and overall performance scores.ResultAI intervention improved overall task performance but was accompanied by an apparent performance-workload paradox, whereby enhanced output coincided with increased neurophysiological and systemic strain. Descriptively, NASA-TLX Overall Perceived Workload decreased from 54.05 to 44.91 during complex tasks, while HRV declined by 48.68% in Task 1, indicating acute autonomic strain. EEG revealed increased BAR in the frontal (F3: 29.2%), parietal (P3), and occipital (O1) regions, suggesting heightened attentional and sensory demands associated with monitoring and verifying AI-generated suggestions.ConclusionAI redistributes rather than eliminates workload, increasing executive verification and visual monitoring demands. Future AI systems for older adults should prioritize cognitive ergonomics to minimize executive burden and sensory strain, preventing premature cognitive fatigue while enhancing task performance and supporting sustainable human-AI interaction.

papers.title: Radiosurgical capsulotomy for treatment-resistant obsessive-compulsive disorder through a network neuroscience lens.
papers.abstract: Severe, treatment-resistant obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD) remains disabling despite optimized pharmacotherapy and exposure and response prevention (ERP). Radiosurgical capsulotomy is an irreversible ablative intervention reserved for highly selected patients. This narrative review examines evidence from structural MRI, diffusion imaging, functional connectivity, electrophysiology, and radiobiology. The search was supplemented by a reproducible PubMed search across eight prespecified modules (856 records before and 739 after deduplication), with an audited 102-record core SRS/OCD set. Structural lesion mapping and a small longitudinal diffusion study support investigating pathway involvement alongside lesion volume, but do not establish a validated network mechanism or individualized targeting biomarker. Functional MRI and EEG findings in OCD and connectivity studies of other interventions provide complementary evidence but require cautious cross-modality extrapolation. Single-session irradiation must be distinguished from thermal capsulotomy; dose, prescription isodose, irradiated volume, and delayed toxicity require joint interpretation. We use "functional disconnection" as a hypothesis concerning downstream effects of tissue injury, not evidence of a nonablative or reversible treatment. Priorities include harmonized longitudinal imaging, dose-volume-connectivity analyses, cognitive and behavioral surveillance, and controlled evaluation of ERP timing. Current evidence supports a network-informed research framework without establishing a post-radiosurgery plasticity window or superiority of connectivity over conventional planning variables.

papers.title: Neuromonitoring of perioperative microembolization and its association with postoperative stroke after carotid endarterectomy.
papers.abstract: This study aims to assess whether perioperative microembolization can identify patients at risk for postoperative stroke. A total of 257 carotid endarterectomy procedures in 254 patients were analyzed (154 symptomatic, 103 asymptomatic). Neuromonitoring, combining transcranial Doppler ultrasonography and continuous electroencephalography, was utilized to evaluate cerebral perfusion and detect microembolic signals (MES). Monitoring covered the entire intraoperative phase and a standardized 20-minute postoperative observation window. Postoperative stroke occurred in seven patients, six of whom were symptomatic prior to the procedure. In exploratory penalized regression analyses, higher postoperative MES counts (OR 1.02 per MES, 95% CI 1.01-1.04; p < 0.001) and an intraoperative burden of ≥ 10 MES (OR 6.06, 95% CI 1.40-34.78; p = 0.016) were associated with postoperative stroke. Symptomatic patients exhibited a significantly higher embolic burden (6.7 ± 13.3 vs. 2.2 ± 5.0, p = 0.004). Beyond its role in guiding selective shunting, transcranial Doppler monitors the occurrence of microembolization, which could serve as a potential indicator of perioperative stroke. In this exploratory analysis, both an intraoperative burden of 10 or more MES and sustained postoperative microembolization were associated with postoperative stroke. Given the low number of events, these findings are hypothesis-generating and require prospective validation before they can guide perioperative management.

papers.title: Neuronal primary cilia are not required for hippocampal circuit function or behavior in adult mice.
papers.abstract: Primary cilia, which are present in most brain cells, are essential for brain development and function. During early brain development, dysfunction of the primary cilia can lead to a broad spectrum of disorders, collectively termed ciliopathies, that include brain malformations and intellectual disability. Although the role of primary cilia in brain development is well-established, cilia-mediated signaling in mature neurons and the contribution of cilia to neuronal circuit function remain controversial. Using mouse genetic and behavioral studies, single-cell electrophysiology, and 2-photon imaging, we show that deletion of primary cilia from adult hippocampal neurons is not required for hippocampal circuit function or behavior. Chronic genetic deletion or acute laser ablation of primary cilia from mature pyramidal neurons in the CA1 or CA3 regions of the hippocampus did not affect neuronal excitability, basal synaptic transmission, or long-term synaptic plasticity at excitatory CA3-CA1 hippocampal synapses. Moreover, the loss of primary cilia did not affect hippocampal-dependent learning and memory or anxiety-like behaviors. These results challenge the prevailing view of cilia function in mature hippocampal neurons and suggest that neuronal cilia in the adult hippocampus do not serve as major signaling hubs for pathways essential for neuronal function or behavior.

papers.title: Taking a clinical history in adolescents and adults presenting with seizures or epilepsy.
papers.abstract: Despite advances in EEG, neuroimaging, and other diagnostic technologies, a carefully obtained clinical history remains the cornerstone of diagnosis, classification, and treatment planning. However, structured guidance on history-taking that integrates state-of-the-art evidence and the updated 2025 International League Against Epilepsy (ILAE) seizure classification is limited. We performed a review of evidence published between January 2000 and April 2026, supplemented by landmark earlier studies, ILAE position papers, and National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE) guidelines. Evidence was synthesized to develop a practical framework for obtaining and interpreting the clinical history in adolescents and adults presenting with a first seizure, recurrent seizures, or established epilepsy. We present a structured approach that follows the sequence of a clinical consultation, encompassing the presenting complaint, detailed event reconstruction, semiology, collateral witness accounts, smartphone video recordings, seizure triggers and temporal patterns, past medical history, medication review, family history, social factors, and safety issues. We discuss the diagnostic value of individual history elements, practical strategies for distinguishing epileptic seizures from functional/dissociative seizures and syncope, and the contribution of history-taking to seizure classification under the updated 2025 ILAE framework. We also summarize clinically relevant risk factors, comorbidities, and management implications that influence diagnostic accuracy and individualized care. Practical diagnostic questionnaires are provided to facilitate differential diagnosis and seizure classification, particularly for clinicians without specialist epilepsy expertise. A systematic clinical history, obtained from the individual and eyewitnesses and complemented by video recordings when available, remains the single most important diagnostic tool in epilepsy. Structured history-taking improves diagnostic accuracy, reduces misdiagnosis, supports accurate seizure classification, guides appropriate investigations, and provides the foundation for personalized management. This practical framework offers an evidence-based approach that can be readily incorporated into routine clinical practice and education across diverse healthcare settings.

papers.title: Viral Strategies for In Vivo Optogenetic Stimulation of Purkinje Cell Terminals and Electrophysiological Characterization of Downstream Cerebellar Nuclear Activity in Mice.
papers.abstract: The cerebellar cortex regulates motor and cognitive function through its sole output neurons, the Purkinje cells (PCs), which inhibit downstream targets, yet precise manipulation of PC activity in vivo remains technically challenging. Here, we describe two viral strategies with differing cell-type specificities for in vivo optogenetic control of PCs and functional assessment of neural activity in downstream target regions. Specifically, we detail strategies for expression of the fast channelrhodopsin ChETA in PCs that enable light-evoked activation of PC axonal terminals in medial deep cerebellar nuclei (mDCN), and demonstrate light-evoked modulation of mDCN neural activity using in vivo extracellular electrophysiology. This protocol provides a reproducible and adaptable framework for cell-type-specific manipulation and functional characterization of cerebellar circuits, with broad applicability to studies of cerebellar physiology, motor and nonmotor behavior, learning and disease. This protocol describes viral strategies for in vivo optogenetic tagging of cerebellar Purkinje cells and extracellular electrophysiological recording of opsin-evoked responses in the medial deep cerebellar nucleus, providing a reproducible approach to investigate cerebellar circuit connectivity and functional interactions with cell-type specificity.

papers.title: Single-Channel Electrophysiology Using a Miniaturized Montal-Mueller Planar Lipid Bilayer System for Recording a Synthetic K2P Channel.
papers.abstract: The functional reconstitution of ion channels into planar lipid bilayers provides a strategy to investigate channel activity at the single-molecule level. However, conventional Montal-Mueller bilayer systems typically require bulky experimental setups, manual chamber assembly, and relatively large recording volumes, which increase reagent consumption and may introduce additional sources of electrical noise due to extended wiring and external headstages. Here, we present a miniaturized, ready-to-use bilayer platform (BLMchipMM) integrated with a compact amplifier that enables stable single-channel recordings with reduced reagent consumption and simplified operation. This protocol describes the use of this system for performing single-channel electrophysiology measurements. Using this system, we reconstituted a synthetic K2P channel (ancTREK1) and used it as a proof-of-principle test protein to validate reconstitution and single-channel recording. Single-channel recordings show a current-voltage relationship in Mg2+-free symmetric K+ solutions, with conductance values consistent with those reported for TREK1 channels. The successful reconstitution of this K2P-like channel demonstrates the utility of this system for single-channel analysis in artificial membranes.

papers.title: Pathogenic Mechanisms of Two Novel Variants in the GJB1 Gene.
papers.abstract: Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease X-linked Type 1 (CMTX1), caused by GJB1 mutations, presents diagnostic challenges due to phenotypic heterogeneity and novel variants. This study reviews clinical data from 2021-2024 and investigates the mechanisms of two novel GJB1 variants. We retrospectively analyzed eight male patients, evaluating clinical signs, electrophysiology, and sural nerve biopsies. Pathogenicity of novel variants was assessed via bioinformatics, ChimeraX molecular modeling, and HeLa cell models focusing on protein localization and channel function (scratch-loading/DAPI assays). Patients showed typical distal muscle atrophy and intermediate conduction velocities; three exhibited rare CNS white matter abnormalities. Two novel variants were identified: c.130dupT and c.124A > G. c.130dupT led to a complete "loss of expression" of the full-length Cx32 protein. c.124A > G resulted in significant cytoplasmic protein retention (p < 0.05). Molecular modeling revealed a physical constriction (1.229 Å) in the channel bottleneck and an increased electrostatic barrier. Functional assays confirmed significant impairment in both gap junction and hemichannel activity (p < 0.01). This study identifies two previously unreported GJB1 variants and elucidates their distinct pathogenic mechanisms: c.130dupT acts through loss of expression, whereas c.124A > G causes functional defect via structural channel constriction. These findings expand the genetic spectrum of CMTX1 and provide a basis for precise molecular diagnosis.

papers.title: Human Th17 state classification reveals a selective vulnerability in acylcarnitine metabolism in type 2 diabetes
papers.abstract: Th17 cells are categorized as non-pathogenic (Th17np) and pathogenic (Th17p), states defined primarily in murine autoimmune models. In contrast, studying these states in humans remains difficult because these subsets lack validated identifiers. We developed a nanovial-based single-cell ELISA to isolate cytokine-secreting human Th17 cells and define Th17np vs Th17p cell transcriptional states. These signatures enabled predictive classification and flow-cytometric identification across tissues and diseases. Application of these strategies with single-cell metabolic modeling and functional profiling revealed that Th17np cells predominate in type 2 diabetes yet exhibit impaired fatty acid oxidation capacity despite elevated carnitine palmitoyltransferase 1A (CPT1A). CRISPR perturbation and pharmacologic inhibition identified acylcarnitine metabolism as a regulator of Th17 state balance and exposed a selective metabolic vulnerability in type 2 diabetes. This framework links human Th17 cell pathogenicity to lipid metabolism.

papers.title: Case Report: Bilateral tonic-clonic seizures as initial presentation of Lhermitte-Duclos Disease and Cowden Syndrome.
papers.abstract: Lhermitte-Duclos Disease is a rare, benign cerebellar tumour that is a manifestation of Cowden Syndrome, a hereditary tumour predisposition syndrome caused by germline mutations in the PTEN gene. Here, we report a 38-year-old female patient with no past medical history or family neurological history presenting to hospital with a new, unprovoked, bilateral tonic-clonic seizure with no apparent seizure focus. EEG showed no epileptiform activity, and 7T MRI demonstrated bilateral Lhermitte-Duclos Disease as well as several cortical meningoencephaloceles. Her seizures were controlled with levetiracetam, and given her cerebellar lesion was minimally symptomatic, no further interventions were pursued. PTEN germline testing identified a heterozygous c.1003C>T (p.Arg335*) variant known to be pathogenic for Cowden Syndrome, and we promptly referred this patient for cancer screening. She was diagnosed with ductal carcinoma in situ and thyroid atypia of undetermined significance, and she subsequently underwent bilateral mastectomy and total thyroidectomy respectively. Lhermitte-Duclos Disease and Cowden Syndrome may present initially in previously healthy patients with bilateral tonic-clonic seizures without clear epileptogenic foci. Recognition of the underlying hereditary cancer syndrome enables timely cancer detection, potentially improving treatment outcomes.

papers.title: Methodology for identification of depleted metallic uranium and natural metallic uranium by portable gamma spectrometer.
papers.abstract: The requirement to distinguish between depleted metallic uranium (DU) and natural metallic uranium (NU) is essential in nuclear forensics, regulatory enforcement, nuclear fuel fabrication and environmental monitoring. Traditional laboratory-based methods offer high accuracy but are impractical for on-site measurement. This research develops a portable gamma spectrometry-based methodology for identifying DU and NU in real-time, non-destructively. The study utilizes a NaI(Tl) based gamma spectrometer to measure characteristic emissions from uranium isotopes and its daughter products. Key gamma peaks, particularly those at 92 keV (234Th) and 186 keV (235U), were analysed to derive isotopic ratios indicative of the material type. Emphasis was given on choosing right gamma peak and adjustment for x-ray contribution in 92 keV peak. Estimated activity ratio of 235U to 234Th of five natural uranium samples was greater than or equal to 0.046 and the activity ratio of five depleted uranium sample found to be less than 0.046, which validated the methodology. The results demonstrate that, with proper calibration, and spectral analysis, portable gamma spectrometry can serve as an effective tool for real-time uranium isotope identification in applications ranging from nuclear safeguards and non-proliferation to environmental monitoring and emergency response.

papers.title: Step-by-Step Protocol for Fluorescence-Based Analysis of Uptake in Transporter-Expressing Xenopus laevis Oocytes.
papers.abstract: Xenopus laevis oocytes are widely used as a heterologous expression system for investigating the function of membrane proteins due to robust expression of heterologous protein and a low endogenous transport background. Traditionally, transporter activity in oocytes has been assessed using electrophysiology or radiolabeled uptake assays, approaches that are constrained by the requirement for electrogenicity of the transport process, availability of radiolabeled compounds, and instrumentation. Here, we describe a fluorescence-based uptake assay that enables direct and rapid quantification of transporter activity using a fluorescence plate reader. The protocol uses the Arabidopsis thaliana sucrose transporter 1 (SUC1) and its fluorescent substrate esculin as a case for how to set up the assay. The workflow includes optimizing assay conditions, sample preparation, fluorescent measurements, and downstream data analysis using R. This method can readily be adapted to other transporter-substrate pairs, and it supports applications such as transporter inhibitor screening, mutational analysis, characterization of kinetic properties, or indirect substrate specificity testing through competition assays. Overall, this protocol provides a simple and scalable alternative to traditional techniques, eliminating the need for radiolabeled compounds or electrophysiology while enabling easy quantitative assessment of transporter activity. Key features • Provides a simple, plate reader-based fluorescence uptake assay for quantifying transporter activity in Xenopus laevis oocytes. • Adaptable to any transporter with a compatible fluorescent substrate, supporting rapid testing of substrate specificity indirectly through competition assays or mutant screening. • Includes a complete workflow from assay setup and conduction to data analysis, suitable for both initial characterization and routine functional testing of membrane transporters.
